sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Emails from my agents are from me
sections.para: Some people read my agents' emails as a chatbot's. They are from me: the agents draft, follow up and collect evidence; I read, change and send every one. It is the Wizard of Oz in reverse. Behind most answers is an article, written once and linked many times. And every part of an email buys the next, so first emails should open with plain text.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: A person behind the agents, an article behind the email
sections.para: People assume a chatbot; the agents draft and I send every email. Kelley's 1984 Wizard of Oz method, reversed. Almost every answer has an article behind it, and if none is ready it is worth writing, which is how a short question gets a long answer that scales. Each part of an email buys the next, so start with plain text.

sections.label: They thought it was a chatbot
sections.line: Why people read them as a chatbot
sections.para: A few correspondents assumed my agents' emails came from a chatbot with nobody reading, because years of support bots taught us chatbots are not clever. That reading changes what people forgive, trust and answer. Who is speaking proposed a line on every email; this article is the fuller answer and the link for the bottom of those emails.

sections.label: The Wizard of Oz, in reverse
sections.line: The Wizard of Oz, in reverse
sections.para: In 1984 J. F. Kelley at IBM named the OZ paradigm: participants believed a program understood them while a hidden person supplied answers, until the program could do without them. My emails reverse it: I say openly that I am behind them, and the person is not phased out, because an email, unlike an article, cannot be undone.

sections.label: What happens behind the curtain
sections.line: Agents draft; I read, think, change and send
sections.para: The correspondence agents draft replies, follow up threads, map what was said into a CRM with sources, collect evidence and track what is owed, and send nothing to the people I write to. I read every draft and use it to think, change it, often a lot, and sometimes ask for an article so the email can be short and point to it.

sections.label: An article behind every email
sections.para: If an email answers a real question, there should almost always be an article behind it, and if none is ready, it is worth writing. Several articles here began as replies. A two-hundred-word email can get two thousand words back, but only once: the next person gets a link, and the article can be forwarded, checked and corrected.

sections.label: Every part of an email buys the next
sections.line: Each part of an email buys the next
sections.para: The subject buys the first line, which buys the paragraph, which buys the email, which buys the article. Inbox previews show the first text, up to about 140 characters. So first emails should open with a plain paragraph that is the whole answer, as the Army's bottom line up front asks, then the banner and detail, a line on who is speaking, and this link.

sections.label: The memo is where the thinking happens
sections.line: The memo is where the thinking happens
sections.para: I started the memo with one idea and finished with three: the curtain, the article behind every email, and how each part of an email buys the next. The agent then checks it against the record. A next article will argue that people who work this way, with agents behind them and an article behind every answer, are highly employable.

sections.label: If you got here from one of my emails
sections.line: If you came here from my email
sections.para: The email was drafted with my agents and sent by me, and I read it before it went. If it was long, the article behind it holds the full answer. The first paragraph should have been enough on its own; if it was not, say so, and the next one will start differently.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: Anecdotes, a proposal and a loose analogy
sections.para: The chatbot reading comes from a few people, not a measurement. The plain-text-first layout is a proposal we are starting to try. Preview length varies by client. Not every email gets an article; the rule is for answers to real questions. And unlike Kelley's participants, my correspondents are told who is behind the curtain.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.para: From my voice memo of 18 October 2026; J. F. Kelley's 1984 paper in ACM Transactions on Office Information Systems, read from the paper; the US Army's AR 25-50 of 2013, read from the archived PDF; and Customer.io on preheader text. Related articles cover who is speaking, the human in the loop and the correspondence agents.
